title: Treaty of Vienna (18 November 1738), settlement of the War of the Polish Succession
exact_locator: Treaty of Vienna 1738, the Neapolitan-Sicilian clauses: Austria cedes the kingdoms of Naples and Sicily to Don Carlos of Bourbon in exchange for Parma and Piacenza
statement: Austria ceded Naples and Sicily to Don Carlos (Charles of Bourbon), who had taken them by conquest in 1734-35; the cession made the Bourbon kingdoms an independent state recognised in European public law.
interpretation: This is the legal title by which the Kingdom of Sicily is a Bourbon possession at the snapshot. It says who holds the island, not where any line runs.
source: Treaty of Vienna 1738 as reported in standard diplomatic histories of the War of the Polish Succession

title: Governing institutions of the Kingdom of Sicily in continuous operation across 1756, as catalogued by the Italian state archives
exact_locator: Guida generale degli Archivi di Stato italiani, Archivio di Stato di Palermo: 'Real segreteria (1611-1826, con docc. dal sec. XVI)'; 'Deputazione del regno (1547-1819)'; 'Deputazione delle strade (1731-1819)'; 'Suprema deputazione generale di salute pubblica (1731-1818)'; 'Giunta poi Deputazione suprema degli ospedali (1750-1818)'
statement: The Bourbon secretariat of state for Sicily, the standing Deputation of the Kingdom (the organ representing the Sicilian Parliament between sessions), and the deputations for roads, public health and hospitals all have archival date ranges that contain 1756-08-01.
interpretation: Government actually running on the island at the snapshot, evidenced by the surviving record series of its own organs rather than by a narrative claim. The Deputazione del regno matters most: Sicily had its own parliament and its own fiscal machinery, which is why it is a separate actor from Naples.
source: Guida generale degli Archivi di Stato italiani, Archivio di Stato di Palermo (Ministero della Cultura)

title: Treaty of The Hague (17 February 1720), concluding the War of the Quadruple Alliance
exact_locator: Treaty of The Hague, 17 February 1720, the Savoy-Austria exchange clause; giving effect to the Treaty of London (1718)
statement: Victor Amadeus II of Savoy ceded Sicily to Austria and received Sardinia in exchange, taking the style King of Sardinia thereafter.
interpretation: The legal title by which the island of Sardinia is a Savoyard possession at the snapshot. Note the symmetry with Sicily: the two islands were swapped between the same two powers, which is why neither island's ownership can be inferred from a dynasty's name.
source: Treaty of The Hague 1720 as reported in standard diplomatic histories of the War of the Quadruple Alliance

title: Savoyard government institutions of the Kingdom of Sardinia in continuous operation across 1756, as catalogued by the Italian state archives
exact_locator: SIAS, Archivio di Stato di Cagliari: 'Segreteria di Stato e di Guerra del Regno di Sardegna (1720-1848)'; 'Reale udienza del Regno di Sardegna (1564-1868)'; 'Antico Archivio Regio (1323-1832)', ordered into 29 categories by the Savoyard monarchy in the eighteenth century
statement: The Savoyard secretariat of state and war for the Kingdom of Sardinia opens in 1720 - the year of the exchange - and runs to 1848; the island's supreme court (Reale udienza) and the royal archive both span the snapshot.
interpretation: The 1720 start date of the Segreteria is the institutional fingerprint of the Hague exchange: a new government apparatus for the island begins exactly when sovereignty changed, and is still running in 1756.
source: SIAS - Sistema Informativo degli Archivi di Stato, Archivio di Stato di Cagliari (Ministero della Cultura)

title: Editti, pregoni ed altri provvedimenti emanati pel Regno di Sardegna dappoiche' passo' sotto la dominazione della Real Casa di Savoia sino all'anno 1774
exact_locator: Cagliari, Reale Stamperia, 1775, compiled by royal command of Victor Amadeus III, ed. Pietro Sanna Lecca; Sardegna Digital Library, LIBRI RARI A048b bis (Biblioteca Regionale di Cagliari)
statement: An official royal compilation of the edicts and pregoni actually promulgated for the Kingdom of Sardinia from the Savoyard accession in 1720 to 1774 - a window that contains the snapshot.
interpretation: Cited for its scope, not merely its title: the compilation exists because a continuous body of law was being issued FOR the island across 1720-1774. No single 1756 edict is quoted here, so this is supporting evidence and is marked as such.
source: Sardegna Digital Library / Biblioteca Regionale di Cagliari, shelfmark LIBRI RARI A048b bis; HathiTrust catalog 008604153

title: Creation of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies
exact_locator: Ferdinand IV of Naples and III of Sicily becomes Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies, 12 December 1816
statement: Until 1816 Naples and Sicily were separate kingdoms, each with their own laws, customs and constitutions; the 1816 act merged them.
interpretation: Recorded so it can never be back-dated. At 1756-08-01 Charles of Bourbon is king of both, but they are two kingdoms, and a shared monarch merges no territory. The merger is sixty years after the snapshot.
source: standard accounts of the creation of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies

title: Fusione perfetta - the 1847 act of Charles Albert merging the island of Sardinia with the mainland Savoyard states
exact_locator: Perfect Fusion, 1847, abolishing the administrative separation between the mainland states and the island
statement: Before 1847 ONLY the island of Sardinia proper was part of the Kingdom of Sardinia; the mainland possessions - Savoy, Piedmont, Nice, Genoa - were held by the Savoys in their own right as a composite monarchy and personal union.
interpretation: This is the decisive one for scope. Authorising only the ISLAND is not a conservative simplification - in 1756 the Kingdom of Sardinia legally IS the island, and Piedmont, Savoy and Nice are a separate composite holding of the same dynasty. Producing them from this actor would be the 1847 state back-dated by ninety years.
source: standard accounts of the Perfect Fusion of 1847

title: Charles of Bourbon succeeds to the Spanish throne and cedes Naples and Sicily to his son Ferdinand
exact_locator: Charles becomes Charles III of Spain, 1759; Naples and Sicily pass to Ferdinand
statement: The Bourbon monarch of Naples and Sicily at the snapshot is Charles; the succession to Ferdinand is three years later.
interpretation: Recorded to fix WHICH monarch is on the throne at 1756-08-01, so no later reign is imported.
source: standard accounts of the Bourbon succession
